prompt.context: A hospital group has been experiencing growing pains and has asked our firm for help. The group originally consisted of one main hospital and then acquired 3 other hospitals. Profits are going down. The CEO of the main hospital recently changed from an MD doctor to an MBA with business experience. No other organizational, market, or external changes have occurred.
prompt.question: The hospital group has asked you to identify the root cause of the profitability decline and recommend a course of action.

clarifying_info.q: What do you mean by growing pains?
clarifying_info.a: The hospital group originally consisted of one hospital and then it acquired 3 other hospitals, and its profits are going down.
Yes, the CEO of the main hospital changed; it was originally an MD doctor, now it is a business experience MBA.

clarifying_info.q: Any other changes or events impacting the hospital group?
Did the acquired hospitals experience a decline in profits?
clarifying_info.a: No, the acquired hospitals did not experience any decline in profits.

clarifying_info.q: What are the revenue streams for the hospital?
clarifying_info.a: The hospital treats patients and mainly collects payments from insurance companies based on the service provided.

clarifying_info.q: Has the volume of patients changed?
Has there been any change in the mix of services performed (e.g., lower number of surgeries)?
Can you explain the insurance coverage categories?
clarifying_info.a: Patients can be categorized as: Private Insurance Covered, Public Insurance Covered, or No Insurance (usually homeless people). Payments from private insurance are greater than from public insurance.

clarifying_info.q: What are the key drivers that bring patients with private insurance to the hospital?
What is the cost of the billing outsourcing service to physicians?
What is the physician's annual profit?
How does the physician spend his/her time?
clarifying_info.a: 75% on patient care, 15% on billing, 10% on administrative overhead.

clarifying_info.q: What is the revenue of the doctor's office?
Does the physician incur additional cost when adding 15% more patient care time (if billing is outsourced)?

exhibits.title: Survey of Doctors regarding hospital
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing the distribution of doctors' opinions about the hospital across three categories: Positive Opinion, No Opinion, and Negative Opinion.

exhibits.title: Issues Impacting Doctors
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing the percentage of doctors citing various issues impacting their practice.

framework: 1. Isolate which entity is driving the profit decline: main hospital vs. acquired hospitals
2. For the declining entity (main hospital), apply P&L split: Revenue vs. Costs
3. If revenue is declining: decompose into Volume x Price/Mix
4. Identify patient mix shift: insurance type (Private vs. Public vs. Uninsured)
5. Identify root cause of mix shift: referral patterns from private physicians
6. Hypothesize link between management change and physician perception/referrals
8. Identify actionable lever: billing outsourcing service as relationship-builder
9. Quantify economics of billing outsourcing for physicians (cost-benefit/ROI)

questions.prompt: Step 1 – Which entity is causing the profit decline: the main hospital or the acquired hospitals?
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask whether the acquired hospitals are also declining. Answer: only the main hospital is declining. This quickly narrows focus to the original hospital, ruling out the acquisition as the primary driver.

questions.prompt: Step 2 – What is driving profitability decline in the main hospital: revenue or costs?
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure along Revenue and Cost drivers. Costs are unchanged. Revenue is declining. Strong candidates articulate this split before diving into specifics.

questions.prompt: Step 3 – What is driving revenue decline?
questions.guidance: Revenue = Volume x Average Revenue per Patient. Volume is unchanged. Therefore average revenue per patient must be declining. This implies the mix of patients (by insurance type) is shifting toward lower-paying insurance categories (public insurance or uninsured).

questions.prompt: Step 4 – Why is the patient mix shifting toward lower-paying insurance?
questions.guidance: Private-insurance patients are driven to the hospital primarily by physician referrals. A shift away from private-insurance patients implies fewer referrals from private physicians. Candidate should hypothesize that physician perception of the hospital has deteriorated following the management change (MD CEO replaced by MBA CEO), leading to fewer referrals.

questions.prompt: Step 5 – How can we test the hypothesis that physician perception has declined?
questions.guidance: Candidate should propose surveying physicians who normally refer patients. Interviewer then directs candidate to Exhibits 1 and 2.

questions.prompt: Step 6 – Interpret Exhibits 1 and 2. What do they tell us, and what is the next step?
questions.guidance: Exhibit 1: ~65% of doctors have No Opinion about the hospital — indifference is bad for referrals even if not outright negative. Combined negative+indifferent is ~85%. Exhibit 2: Billing Complexity is the #1 issue cited by ~70% of doctors. Key insight: physician indifference and billing complexity are the primary pain points. The hospital has an outsourced billing service it does not aggressively market — this is an opportunity to deepen physician relationships and solve their top pain point.

questions.prompt: Step 7 – The hospital offers a billing outsourcing service at $50,000/year to physicians. Assess whether this is a viable offering. Calculate ROI, new physician profit, and increase in profit %.
questions.guidance: Candidate should map out the logic before calculating: (1) If the physician outsources billing, the 15% of time freed up can be used for additional patient care. (2) That additional patient care generates incremental revenue. (3) Compare incremental revenue gain vs. cost of the service to derive ROI and new profit. Candidate must ask for the physician's revenue figure ($425,000) to complete the calculation.

math.setup: Physician financials: Revenue = $425,000; Profit = $175,000; Cost = $250,000. Time allocation: 75% patient care, 15% billing, 10% admin. If billing outsourced, physician can redirect 15% of time to patient care.
steps: Incremental revenue from redirecting billing time to patient care: $425,000 × (15% / 75%) = $85,000

brainstorming.prompt: What are the ways the main hospital can rebuild and strengthen its relationships with private physicians?

categories.name: Communication & Engagement
ideas: Regular physician liaison meetings with hospital leadership
Dedicated physician relations officer or program
Invite physicians to hospital advisory boards or committees

categories.name: Service & Operational Improvements
ideas: Aggressively market the billing outsourcing service ($50K, 70% ROI for physicians)
Offer co-management arrangements for service lines
Provide dedicated scheduling lanes for physician-referred patients

categories.name: Incentives & Programs
ideas: Physician loyalty programs or preferred-partner designations
Joint revenue-sharing arrangements for aligned service lines
Continuing medical education (CME) events hosted by hospital
Subsidized malpractice or liability insurance programs

categories.name: Quality & Reputation
ideas: Publicize quality metrics and outcomes data to physician community
Seek and promote hospital accreditations relevant to referred specialties
Highlight any awards or recognitions under new management

recommendation: The main hospital is experiencing a revenue decline because the mix of patients is shifting away from private-insurance patients toward lower-paying public insurance or uninsured patients.

The root cause is a decline in physician referrals of private-insurance patients, likely driven by physician indifference or dissatisfaction following the management change from an MD CEO to an MBA CEO.
Survey data (Exhibits 1 & 2) confirms ~85% of physicians are indifferent or negative about the hospital, with billing complexity cited as the top issue by ~70% of physicians.

The hospital should aggressively market its existing billing outsourcing service to private physicians at $50,000/year — this delivers a 70% ROI and a 20% profit increase for physicians, making it a highly compelling value proposition that simultaneously strengthens physician relationships and rebuilds referral volume.
risks: Physicians may already be entrenched with competing hospitals and resistant to re-engagement
Billing outsourcing alone may not overcome broader perception issues tied to management change
If the MBA CEO's operational changes negatively impacted clinical quality, physician concerns may run deeper than billing complexity
Market share loss may take time to reverse even after relationship improvement begins
next_steps: Conduct a broader physician satisfaction survey to quantify the scale of the referral decline and identify any additional pain points beyond billing
Launch a targeted physician outreach program led by the CEO or a physician liaison to personally re-engage top referring doctors
Pilot the billing outsourcing service with a select group of physicians and track referral volume changes
Set a 6-month milestone to measure change in patient mix (private vs. public insurance) as a proxy for referral recovery
Evaluate whether the new CEO's management approach requires adjustment to better align with physician community expectations
